title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: Given an array of points on the plane, where points[i] = [xi, yi], and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by Euclidean distance. The answer may be returned in any order, and it is guaranteed to be unique except for the order.
realWorld: The 'nearest N' query behind a store locator or a driver-dispatch service: you hold millions of candidate locations and need the five nearest to a rider, not a ranking of all of them. The same bounded-heap selection is how a vector search index keeps the k best candidates while streaming over far more vectors than it could ever sort.

examples.explanation: Squared distances are 1 + 9 = 10 and 4 + 4 = 8. The second point is nearer, and no square root was needed to find that out.

Squared distances are 18, 26 and 20. The two smallest are 18 and 20. Note that the farthest point, [5,-1], is the one the size-2 heap keeps at its root until it is evicted — the root is always the worst of the survivors, never the best.
When k equals the number of points, the whole input is the answer and no eviction ever happens. Ties in distance are allowed; either order is accepted.

constraints: Squared distances therefore never exceed 2 * 10^8, which fits comfortably in an int

bruteForce.whySlow: The sort settles the relative order of every pair of points, but the answer only needs to know which side of the k-th boundary each point falls on. With n = 10^4 and k = 5, the comparisons that decide which of two far-away points is marginally nearer — points neither of which will ever be returned — are pure waste, and they are almost all of the comparisons performed. You paid to rank 10^4 items and then threw 99.95% of the ranking away.

patternIdentification: Whenever the question is 'the best k of n' and n is much larger than k, you never need the full order: keep a bounded collection of exactly k items and ask one question of each arriving element — 'does it beat the worst thing I am currently keeping?'. The collection must be ordered *against* the answer, which is the inversion people get backwards: to keep the k closest points you need instant access to the farthest one you are keeping, so it is a MAX-heap on distance. To keep the k largest values (as in kth-largest-element and top-k-frequent) you need instant access to the smallest one you are keeping, so it is a MIN-heap. The root is always the candidate for eviction, never the answer.

optimized.idea: Carry a max-heap ordered by squared distance, capped at size k. Every new point is compared against the heap's root — the farthest point currently kept. If the newcomer is nearer, evict the root and insert it; otherwise it cannot possibly be in the answer, so discard it immediately. Compare squared distances: the square root is a monotone function, so it changes no ordering and only costs time.

commonMistakes: Building the size-k heap as a MIN-heap on distance — `peek()` is then the *closest* point kept, so every eviction throws away the best answer found so far. With points [[1,3],[-2,2],[2,-2]] and k = 2 it returns [[-2,2],[1,3]] when [1,3] is the farthest of the three.

Calling `keep.peek()` before the size check — on the very first point the heap is empty, `peek()` returns null, and dereferencing it throws NullPointerException. The size test has to come first, in the same `if`/`else if` chain.

Assuming the returned collection is sorted by distance. A PriorityQueue's `toArray` and its iterator yield internal heap order, not sorted order; only `poll()` comes out in order. A solution that relies on the first element being the nearest passes a spot check and fails the moment the grader compares position by position.
